slide: Subtitle: Goal-First Planning for new managers
narration: You come in early. You leave late. Your team is busy all day. Every task on the list gets done.
And still, at the end of the month, your manager asks: why aren't we where we need to be?
If that sounds familiar, this course is for you.
Here is a problem that shows up again and again, in almost every team.
People are very good at doing tasks. Fewer people know where the task came from, or why it exists at all.
When you don't know why a task exists, you keep doing it even after it stops helping anyone.

slide: A task is not a goal.
A task is a way to reach a goal.
narration: So let's start with the most important idea in this course.
A goal is the end state. It is what has to be true when we're done.
A task is an action. It is one possible way to get there.
Goals stay. Tasks can change, be added or be dropped, as long as we still reach the goal.

slide: Goal: Everyone who eats is full
narration: Let's make this simple. It's nine in the morning, and lunch needs to happen.
Most people would say the goal is to make lunch. But that's a task.
The goal is: everyone who eats will be full.

Notice what changed. Once the goal is clear, cooking is just one option. You could heat leftovers. You could order in. If there's no food and no money, you could find a place that gives out free meals.
The task changed. The goal didn't.

slide: Your manager hands you a task.
Question: which goal does it serve?
narration: Now take this to work. As a new manager, you live between two levels.
Above you, someone hands you tasks. Below you, your team waits for you to hand them tasks.
If you pass tasks down without the goal behind them, your team will do exactly what you said, even when the situation changes and it no longer makes sense.
If they know the goal, they can adapt on their own.

slide: By the end of this course:
What you'll be able to do
1. Turn any assignment into a clear goal
2. See the full picture before you plan
3. Give your team tasks, and the goal behind them
4. Adapt when things change, without losing the goal
narration: By the end of this course, you'll be able to take any assignment from your manager and turn it into a clear goal.
You'll see the full picture before you start planning.
You'll give your team tasks, and the goal behind them.
And when things change, and they will, you'll adapt without losing the goal.
The method behind all of this is called Goal-First Planning. It's built on principles military planners have used for a long time, adapted for everyday work.

slide: A restaurant kitchen on a busy Saturday night
A real challenge from your own team
narration: You won't just watch. After most lessons there's a short exercise.
In the middle of the course you'll run a busy restaurant kitchen on a Saturday night. At the end, you'll organize a football tournament, with surprises along the way.
And finally, you'll run the whole method on a real challenge from your own team.
Before the next lesson, take a few minutes for your first exercise. It's waiting for you right after this video.
See you there.
Before we go further, here's how this course works, so you can get the most out of it.
Every lesson is short and covers one idea.
If you have ten minutes, you can finish a lesson and its exercise.

slide: Some take two minutes. Some take twenty.
narration: After most lessons there's an exercise. Some take two minutes. Some take twenty.
The exercises are where the method stops being an idea and becomes a habit. Please don't skip them.
We'll start with simple, everyday examples, like getting lunch on the table.
Then we'll move to work. Later you'll run a restaurant kitchen on a busy night, and at the end, a football tournament.
Each example is a little more complex than the one before.

narration: One more thing. Think of a real challenge from your work right now. A project, an assignment, a team problem.
Keep it in mind as we go. By the end of the course, you'll plan it from start to finish.

In this exercise you'll practice the first idea of the course: a task is not a goal.
Download the worksheet from the resources of this lesson.

slide: Part 1: Ten sentences. Goal or task?
narration: In part one, you'll read ten sentences and decide whether each one is a goal or a task.
Remember: a goal is the end state, what has to be true when you're done. A task is an action, one way to get there.
In part two, you'll take your own to-do list and ask one question about every item: which goal does this serve?
It takes about ten minutes. When you're done, check your answers with the answer key.

worksheet.title: Exercise 1: Task or Goal?
worksheet.instructions: Part 1. Mark each sentence as a Goal (an end state: what has to be true when you're done) or a Task (an action: one way to get there).
items: Everyone on the team knows the new process.
Customers who call get an answer the same day.
Book a meeting room for the training.
The new hire can work on their own.
Update the slides for the client meeting.
Every guest at the event is seated before it starts.
All the team's laptops work on Monday morning.
answers: Goal. It describes what is true at the end.
Task. An action. The goal behind it might be: the people who read it know where the project stands.
Goal. It describes what is true for every customer who calls.
Task. An action. The goal behind it might be: the team can use the new tool.
Goal. An end state you can picture.
Task. An action. The goal behind it might be: the client agrees to the next step.
Goal. It describes the moment when it is done.
Task. An action. The goal behind it might be: we buy at a price we can afford.
Goal. It describes what is true on Monday morning.
Task, even though it sounds big. Hiring is an action. The goal behind it might be: design work gets done on time. Sometimes there is another way to reach that goal.

part2.title: Part 2: Reverse derivation
steps: Write down five items from your to-do list for this week.
Next to each item, write the goal it serves.
Mark the items with no clear goal. For each one, decide: drop it, change it, or ask your manager what it is for.
